name: Mid-forehead brow lift

lead: A mid-forehead brow lift is one of several surgical techniques for raising the eyebrows. The surgeon removes a strip of skin and underlying tissue through an incision hidden in a deep horizontal forehead crease, which pulls the brow upward. A higher brow can make the eyes look more open and the upper eyelid area less heavy, and it can smooth the forehead.

It is a classic approach for people with brow ptosis (low-set or drooping brows) who also have thick brows or deep forehead lines that can camouflage the scar. Newer endoscopic and non-surgical options are used more often, but the mid-forehead technique remains in the surgical literature as a direct, well-established option.

paras: Candidates are assessed by a facial plastic, oculoplastic or plastic surgeon, who considers brow position, forehead creases, skin thickness and hairline. The operation is done in an operating setting, with the incision following a natural crease. Combining it with eyelid surgery is common, since brow position affects how much upper eyelid skin appears. Recovery and scar healing are managed by the surgeon.

As with other brow lifts, risks include a visible scar, numbness or altered sensation of the forehead, asymmetry, bleeding and infection. Reference summaries note that direct and hairline approaches carry particular trade-offs, such as numbness and higher revision rates respectively. Anyone considering surgery should discuss them with a qualified surgeon.

angle.text: A mid-forehead brow lift raises the brow position by surgical excision through a forehead crease. People choose it for a more open, less heavy upper eye area.

lead: A mid-forehead brow lift is a surgical approach to brow ptosis, the lowered position of the eyebrow that can interfere with appearance or vision. [1] The incision is made within a deep forehead crease, and the procedure is one of several brow lift variations that also include coronal, endoscopic, pretrichial, temporal, direct and transblepharoplasty approaches. [2]

For appearance, the chain is: removing tissue lifts the brow, a higher brow opens the eye area, and the upper face looks less tired or heavy. StatPearls notes that brow ptosis is diagnosed largely on the examining surgeon's judgement and experience, since a brow level considered low in one person may be acceptable in another. [1]

Comparison with other techniques is part of the literature. Endoscopic lifts are the most commonly used today, coronal lifts fell from favor after popularity in the 1980s and 1990s, and botulinum toxin injections are a non-surgical alternative repeated every four to six months. [2]

paras: Brow ptosis occurs when the lower position of the brow interferes with aesthetics or function, and there is no strict numerical definition. [1] In the mid-forehead approach, the incision follows a deep horizontal forehead crease so the scar can be concealed in the line. [1][2]

The endoscopic approach uses three to five small incisions with a camera and is the most commonly used. Coronal lifts use a long scalp incision. Direct, pretrichial (hairline), temporal and transblepharoplasty approaches place incisions elsewhere. [2] Botulinum toxin injections are a non-surgical option and are sometimes used after surgery to refine results. [2] Radiofrequency and ultrasound devices are being studied for a non-surgical eyebrow lift in a registered trial. [3]

Summaries of brow lift techniques state that complications are rare and minor with a trained surgeon, but list infection and bleeding as risks of any surgery. Hairline lifts have the highest revision rates, direct lifts most often cause numbness, and hair loss is most common after endoscopic lifts. [2] Mid-forehead specific risks include a visible forehead scar.
No studies found specific to the mid-forehead technique beyond a StatPearls overview. [1] A registered trial examines a device for non-surgical eyebrow lift. [3]
